name: Cinnabar-Gyre
description: Cinnabar-Gyre burns low and red against its neighboring asteroid belt, wrapped in cloud bands the color of mercurial blood. Around its north pole spins a permanent gyre—a whirlpool of storm wide enough to swallow three worlds—its spiral arms combed into perfect concentric curves. Scarlet lightning stitches between the bands in threads that glow for minutes at a time.

Even at safe altitude, cockpit thermometers climb and the air recyclers taste of hot metal. The planet's voice is a steady drumbeat of thunder merged into one unbroken roll, and pilots report dreams of red spirals after long watch rotations. Sunlight arrives already strained through the belt's dust, so noon here looks like dusk elsewhere.

Navigation computers refuse to plot straight lines near the gyre: gravity wells bloom and dissolve around the pole, tugging probes into corkscrew descents they do not survive. One recovered probe returned data containing a repeating sequence of prime numbers that matches nothing in any registry. The sequence updates itself with every pass.

Harvesters brave the outer bands for helium-3, but the true prize lies higher: dark crystals nucleating in the cold shear zones, worth more than their mass in warships. Every attempt to map the gravity wells has failed, as if the planet rearranges them out of spite. The navy has quietly begun classifying the prime sequence, which worries the people who noticed.
